---
title: "Forked execution"
engine: julia
format:
  gfm: default
---

A linear instruction program describes one path through a decay tree. When two
paths share the same first frame transformation, evaluating them independently
repeats that work:

```text
root → left child
root → right child
```

[`Fork`](@ref) expresses the tree directly. The instructions before the fork
run once, then every branch starts from the same parent state.

## A two-branch decay

Start with four vectors and name the shared and branch-specific transforms:

```{julia}
#| label: fork-setup
using InstructionalDecayTrees
using FourVectors

objects = (
    FourVector(0.40, 0.10, 0.20; M = 0.30),
    FourVector(-0.20, 0.25, -0.10; M = 0.40),
    FourVector(0.05, -0.30, 0.35; M = 0.20),
    FourVector(-0.10, -0.10, -0.25; M = 0.50),
)

root = ToHelicityFrame((1, 2, 3, 4))
left = (
    ToHelicityFrame((1, 2)),
    MeasureCosThetaPhi(:left, 1),
)
right = (
    ToHelicityFrameParticle2((3, 4)),
    MeasureCosThetaPhi(:right, 3),
)
nothing
```

The familiar approach evaluates two complete root-to-child paths:

```{julia}
#| label: independent-paths
_, left_results =
    apply_decay_instruction((root, left...), objects)
_, right_results =
    apply_decay_instruction((root, right...), objects)

(left = left_results.left, right = right_results.right)
```

The tree-shaped program spells out the common prefix only once:

```{julia}
#| label: shared-prefix-program
program = (
    root,
    Fork((left, right)),
)

parent_state, results = apply_decay_instruction(program, objects)

@assert results.left == left_results.left
@assert results.right == right_results.right
results
```

The state returned by `Fork` is the state that entered it. This lets execution
continue in the parent frame after the branches and avoids choosing either
child as the final frame.

## Counting the saved work

The execution API is backend-agnostic, so a tiny counting backend makes the
shared-prefix property visible. `CountStep` represents an expensive transform;
`RecordState` exposes the state reached by a path.

```{julia}
#| label: counting-backend
struct CountStep{C} <: InstructionalDecayTrees.AbstractInstruction
    counter::C
end

function InstructionalDecayTrees.apply_decay_instruction(step::CountStep, state)
    step.counter[] += 1
    return (state + 1, (;))
end

struct RecordState{Tag} <: InstructionalDecayTrees.AbstractMeasureInstruction end

function InstructionalDecayTrees.apply_decay_instruction(
    ::RecordState{Tag},
    state,
) where {Tag}
    return (state, NamedTuple{(Tag,)}((state,)))
end
nothing
```

Two independent paths execute the common transform twice:

```{julia}
#| label: count-independent-paths
counter = Ref(0)
step = CountStep(counter)

apply_decay_instruction((step, RecordState{:left}()), 0)
apply_decay_instruction((step, RecordState{:right}()), 0)

@assert counter[] == 2
counter[]
```

Putting the transform before a fork executes it once, while both branches
observe the transformed state:

```{julia}
#| label: count-forked-program
counter[] = 0
counted_program = (
    step,
    Fork((
        (RecordState{:left}(),),
        (RecordState{:right}(),),
    )),
)

final_state, counted_results =
    apply_decay_instruction(counted_program, 0)

@assert counter[] == 1
@assert final_state == 1
@assert counted_results == (left = 1, right = 1)
(transforms = counter[], results = counted_results)
```

For a chain with $N$ vertices, independent root-to-vertex paths repeat roughly
$0 + 1 + \cdots + (N - 1)$ frame descents. A nested forked program can visit
each tree edge once instead.

## Branch and result semantics

Branches run in tuple order and may contain instructions, tuples,
[`CompositeInstruction`](@ref)s, or nested forks. Measurements are merged into
one flat `NamedTuple`. Tags must be unique throughout a program containing a
fork; duplicate tags raise `ArgumentError`.

Each branch starts from [`fork_branch_state`](@ref) applied to the parent state.
The default is `deepcopy`, which protects mutable backend states from sibling
changes. This function is public because it is a backend extension point:
immutable or persistent-state backends may overload it to return the original
state. Ordinary application code does not need to call it.

The program tree and state flow retain concrete tuple types, so Julia can
specialize on a statically shaped fork. Built-in measurement tags are runtime
`Symbol`s, however, so the exact `NamedTuple` field names are not encoded in the
measurement instruction type. That inference boundary also applies to linear
programs; it is not introduced by `Fork`. Backends that encode tags as type
parameters, like `RecordState` above, can infer the complete result shape.
